title: Noninvasive Brain Imaging and Stimulation in Post-Stroke Motor Rehabilitation: Mechanisms, Modalities, and Translational Perspectives

subsections.section_title: Foundations of Post-Stroke Motor Recovery and Neurorehabilitation
subsections.subsection_title: Clinical burden and characterization of post-stroke motor deficits
subsections.content:
Motor impairment is among the most prevalent and disabling consequences of stroke, affecting independence, community participation, and long-term quality of life. Global epidemiological analyses indicate that stroke remains a leading cause of adult disability, with motor deficits constituting a major share of the chronic burden ref [1], ref [2]. In prospective cohorts, arm paresis is especially common in the acute stage, and many patients continue to exhibit substantial upper-limb limitation months later despite standard care ref [3], ref [4].

Clinically, post-stroke motor deficits span weakness, loss of dexterity, abnormal muscle synergies, spasticity, impaired coordination, gait dysfunction, and reduced postural control. These deficits are heterogeneous because lesion size and location variably disrupt corticospinal, corticobulbar, cerebellar, and distributed sensorimotor networks. Upper-extremity impairment is often more persistent than lower-extremity impairment, and recovery trajectories differ across body segments and severity strata ref [4], ref [5]. Standardized scales such as the Fugl-Meyer Assessment and the Action Research Arm Test are therefore central for quantifying impairment and activity limitation and for stratifying patients in rehabilitation studies ref [6], ref [7].

Importantly, initial motor severity is one of the strongest predictors of later function, although age, comorbidity, neglect, somatosensory loss, and corticospinal tract damage also influence outcome ref [8], ref [5]. This clinical heterogeneity motivates biomarker-driven approaches that combine behavioral phenotyping with imaging and neurophysiology to better define residual motor system integrity and personalize intervention selection.

subsections.section_title: Foundations of Post-Stroke Motor Recovery and Neurorehabilitation
subsections.subsection_title: Neuroanatomical and network basis of motor dysfunction
subsections.content:
Post-stroke motor dysfunction reflects damage not only to focal cortical or subcortical motor regions but also to the distributed corticospinal and cortico-subcortical systems that support movement. Lesion burden within the corticospinal tract is a major determinant of paresis severity, particularly when infarcts interrupt descending fibers from primary motor, premotor, and supplementary motor areas ref [9], ref [10]. Beyond weakness, impaired dexterity and abnormal synergies can arise from injury to parallel motor pathways and their interactions with sensory and associative regions that normally shape motor planning and execution ref [11].

At the systems level, stroke perturbs large-scale network organization. Functional imaging studies show that unilateral motor deficits are associated with reduced recruitment and disrupted connectivity within the ipsilesional sensorimotor network, accompanied by abnormal overactivity in contralesional motor cortices ref [12], ref [13]. This imbalance has often been interpreted in terms of altered interhemispheric inhibition between homologous motor areas, although its behavioral significance varies with lesion location and impairment severity ref [14]. Damage to structurally strategic hubs can therefore produce deficits disproportionate to lesion size by disconnecting distributed motor circuits.

Network disruption extends beyond primary motor areas to thalamocortical, cerebellar, and frontoparietal loops that contribute to motor selection, adaptation, and sensory guidance. Resting-state and connectomic analyses indicate that the integrity of spared structural and functional connections helps explain inter-individual variation in impairment and recovery potential better than lesion topography alone ref [15], ref [16]. This network-based view provides a key rationale for pairing neuroimaging with neuromodulation to identify residual circuit capacity and target maladaptive patterns of reorganization.

subsections.section_title: Foundations of Post-Stroke Motor Recovery and Neurorehabilitation
subsections.subsection_title: Mechanisms of spontaneous recovery and neuroplasticity
subsections.content:
Spontaneous motor recovery after stroke is most prominent in the first weeks to months and reflects a biological window in which edema resolves, diaschisis diminishes, and spared cortical–subcortical pathways are re-engaged. Across impairment domains, a substantial fraction of recovery follows a proportional pattern tied to the integrity of descending motor systems, particularly the corticospinal tract, although this rule is less evident in patients with severe structural disconnection ref [5], ref [17]. These observations support the view that early behavioral gains are constrained by lesion topology and residual network capacity rather than by lesion volume alone.

At the neural level, recovery depends on experience-dependent plasticity within distributed motor networks. Animal and human studies indicate that peri-infarct cortex undergoes dendritic remodeling, synaptogenesis, and map reorganization, while surviving ipsilesional premotor and supplementary motor areas can assume greater control over movement ref [18], ref [19]. Longitudinal imaging further shows that the restoration of more normal activation patterns in ipsilesional sensorimotor regions is associated with better outcomes, whereas persistent reliance on diffuse contralesional recruitment is often a marker of greater impairment rather than an optimal compensatory state ref [20], ref [21].

Interhemispheric interactions also evolve during recovery. Early after stroke, reduced inhibition from the damaged to the intact hemisphere and increased transcallosal suppression of ipsilesional M1 may contribute to motor deficits, but the functional significance of this imbalance varies with severity and stage ref [22]. More broadly, recovery is now understood as reconnection of large-scale structural and functional networks, with corticospinal integrity, cortical excitability, and sensorimotor connectivity jointly shaping an individual’s capacity for restitution versus compensation ref [17], ref [23].

subsections.section_title: Foundations of Post-Stroke Motor Recovery and Neurorehabilitation
subsections.subsection_title: Principles of motor rehabilitation after stroke
subsections.content:
Motor rehabilitation after stroke is grounded in task-specific, repetitive practice designed to drive use-dependent plasticity within residual corticospinal and distributed sensorimotor networks. Contemporary frameworks emphasize high training intensity, salience, progressive challenge, and active problem solving rather than passive movement alone, because skill acquisition and retention depend on experience-dependent remodeling of motor representations ref [24], ref [25]. Early mobilization and structured therapy are generally encouraged, but the optimal dose, timing, and content must be individualized to neurological severity, medical stability, and fatigue.

A central principle is to align treatment with impairment profile and recovery stage. Interventions may target restitution of premorbid movement patterns, compensation using preserved effectors, or a staged combination of both. Evidence-based approaches such as constraint-induced movement therapy for selected upper-limb patients, body-weight-supported or task-oriented gait training, strength and aerobic exercise, and mirror or mental practice all seek to increase meaningful practice and learned nonuse reduction ref [26], ref [27], ref [28]. Multidisciplinary guidelines therefore recommend goal-directed training that is intensive, functionally relevant, and embedded in everyday activities ref [29].

Rehabilitation is increasingly conceived as precision therapy: outcomes depend on lesion burden, corticospinal tract integrity, cognitive status, and environmental support. Prognostic algorithms based on bedside motor signs and neurophysiology can help match patients to realistic treatment targets and dosing, while biomarkers may identify those most likely to benefit from adjunctive technologies such as robotics, noninvasive stimulation, or neuroimaging-guided interventions ref [30], ref [31]. This stratified view provides the conceptual bridge from conventional therapy principles to imaging- and stimulation-informed neurorehabilitation.

subsections.section_title: Foundations of Post-Stroke Motor Recovery and Neurorehabilitation
subsections.subsection_title: Rationale for integrating imaging and stimulation technologies
subsections.content:
The rationale for combining noninvasive imaging with brain stimulation in post-stroke rehabilitation is that motor deficits arise from distributed network disruption rather than from lesion location alone. Functional MRI and related network measures showed that interhemispheric and ipsilesional motor-system connectivity are closely linked to impairment and recovery, suggesting that stimulation targets should be selected with reference to residual network organization rather than by anatomy alone ref [32], ref [33]. This perspective also aligns with evidence that patterns of cortical recruitment after stroke differ across patients and evolve over time, implying that a fixed stimulation approach is unlikely to suit all recovery stages ref [34].

Imaging can therefore serve at least three translational functions: stratifying patients, localizing viable cortical targets, and providing biomarkers of treatment response. Structural and physiological measures of corticospinal tract integrity, particularly when combined with transcranial magnetic stimulation, improve prediction of upper-limb potential and help define whether ipsilesional facilitation, contralesional suppression, or alternative network engagement is most plausible ref [35], ref [36]. At the same time, stimulation offers a mechanistic probe to test causal contributions of candidate regions identified by imaging, moving beyond correlational descriptions of reorganization ref [37].

This integrated framework is especially important because stimulation effects are state dependent and heterogeneous. Consensus recommendations emphasize that lesion characteristics, baseline excitability, and network status shape responsiveness to transcranial direct current stimulation and repetitive TMS ref [38]. More recently, connectome-based analyses have shown that stroke deficits and recovery trajectories are constrained by structural disconnection, reinforcing the need for individualized imaging-guided neuromodulation rather than one-size-fits-all protocols ref [39].

subsections.section_title: Noninvasive Brain Imaging Modalities for Assessing Motor Recovery
subsections.subsection_title: Structural magnetic resonance imaging and lesion mapping
subsections.content:
Structural MRI provides the anatomical foundation for studying post-stroke motor deficits by delineating infarct location, volume, and involvement of critical cortical and subcortical motor regions. Early work showed that lesion topography is often more informative than total lesion size, particularly when damage affects the primary motor cortex, internal capsule, corona radiata, or basal ganglia pathways that support corticospinal output ref [40], ref [41]. High-resolution T1-, T2-, and FLAIR-based imaging is therefore routinely used to define lesion masks and characterize concomitant atrophy or ventricular enlargement that may reflect broader network injury.

Voxel-based lesion-symptom mapping and related lesion-overlap approaches have strengthened causal inference by linking specific damaged territories to motor impairment. In chronic stroke, residual motor deficits are strongly associated with injury to the corticospinal tract and descending motor fibers, while multivariate lesion-behavior frameworks further indicate that distributed lesion patterns can outperform single-region metrics for explaining upper-limb impairment ref [42], ref [43]. These approaches complement conventional region-of-interest analyses by quantifying how structural disconnection constrains recovery potential.

Beyond cross-sectional impairment mapping, structural MRI contributes to prognosis and treatment stratification. Biomarkers such as corticospinal tract lesion load, overlap with canonical motor pathways, and indices of secondary degeneration have been associated with later motor outcome and responsiveness to rehabilitation ref [44], ref [45]. Nonetheless, lesion mapping alone incompletely captures diaschisis, compensatory reorganization, and premorbid variability, motivating its integration with diffusion and functional imaging in multimodal recovery models ref [46].

subsections.section_title: Noninvasive Brain Imaging Modalities for Assessing Motor Recovery
subsections.subsection_title: Diffusion imaging and white matter integrity
subsections.content:
Diffusion-weighted MRI provides a sensitive window onto post-stroke white-matter injury, particularly within descending motor pathways. Measures derived from diffusion tensor imaging, such as fractional anisotropy and diffusivity, are widely used to index corticospinal tract (CST) degeneration, interhemispheric callosal disruption, and secondary diaschisis remote from the infarct. Early work showed that diffusion abnormalities along the CST correlate with motor impairment and reflect Wallerian degeneration after subcortical stroke ref [47], while tract-specific quantification has since been linked to upper-limb deficit severity and chronic outcome ref [48].

Beyond simple lesion location, diffusion imaging supports network-level models of motor recovery. Integrity of the ipsilesional CST is one of the most reproducible imaging biomarkers of residual motor capacity, and diffusion metrics often outperform lesion volume alone for explaining behavioral variance ref [49]. Tractography studies further indicate that preserved transcallosal and premotor-parietal connections contribute to compensatory reorganization, whereas severe CST damage constrains response to restorative therapies ref [50]. These observations underpin stratification approaches such as the PREP algorithm, in which CST microstructure complements clinical and neurophysiological measures for predicting arm recovery ref [51].

Methodologically, contemporary studies increasingly move beyond tensor-based summaries toward along-tract profiling, crossing-fiber models, and structural connectomics, which better capture complex post-stroke disconnection. Large cohort analyses using disconnectome or connectome frameworks show that distributed white-matter damage, rather than focal CST injury alone, influences motor deficits and recovery trajectories ref [52], ref [39]. Nevertheless, diffusion biomarkers remain sensitive to acquisition choices, edema, and tractography uncertainty, and standardization will be important for translation into multicenter prognostic and treatment-selection pipelines ref [53].

subsections.section_title: Noninvasive Brain Imaging Modalities for Assessing Motor Recovery
subsections.subsection_title: Functional magnetic resonance imaging of motor networks
subsections.content:
Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) has been central to mapping how stroke perturbs distributed motor networks beyond the structural lesion itself. Task-based studies consistently show that hand movement after stroke is accompanied by abnormal recruitment of ipsilesional premotor regions, supplementary motor area, and often contralesional sensorimotor cortex, with the degree and pattern of overactivation depending on impairment severity and recovery stage ref [54], ref [11]. Early work further suggested that greater activation in secondary motor areas may reflect compensatory processing when corticospinal output from primary motor cortex is compromised ref [55].

A major theme in the fMRI literature is the balance between adaptive reorganization and maladaptive interhemispheric interactions. In well-recovered patients, restoration of more lateralized activity within the ipsilesional primary sensorimotor cortex is often associated with better performance, whereas persistent reliance on contralesional motor areas is more common in severe deficits ref [11], ref [56]. Network-level analyses reinforced this view by showing reduced functional connectivity within the ipsilesional motor system and altered coupling between homologous motor cortices after stroke ref [57]. Resting-state fMRI is particularly attractive in impaired patients because it avoids task performance confounds and can quantify spontaneous connectivity within motor networks ref [58].

Clinically, fMRI-derived metrics have been explored as biomarkers of treatment response and prognosis. Longitudinal studies indicate that rehabilitation-related gains can be accompanied by shifts toward more normalized motor-network activation and connectivity ref [59], while early connectivity measures between ipsilesional motor regions and the wider network may help predict later motor outcome ref [58], ref [60]. Nonetheless, interpretation remains challenging because BOLD responses are influenced by vascular reactivity, lesion location, and task difficulty, which can obscure whether observed activation changes reflect true neural recovery or altered neurovascular coupling.

subsections.section_title: Noninvasive Brain Imaging Modalities for Assessing Motor Recovery
subsections.subsection_title: Electroencephalography and magnetoencephalography
subsections.content:
Electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG) provide millisecond-scale measures of cortical dynamics and are therefore well suited to characterizing post-stroke motor network dysfunction beyond what can be inferred from structural injury alone. In chronic stroke, movement-related desynchronization and rebound in the mu/beta bands are often attenuated or spatially reorganized over sensorimotor cortex, reflecting impaired recruitment of ipsilesional motor areas and compensatory contralesional engagement. These oscillatory abnormalities can be captured during attempted movement, motor imagery, or resting state, and have been linked to residual impairment and treatment responsiveness ref [61], ref [62].

A major contribution of EEG/MEG has been the quantification of interhemispheric imbalance after stroke. Studies combining transcranial magnetic stimulation with EEG have shown altered effective connectivity and abnormal propagation of cortical responses from the affected hemisphere, providing a physiological index of network disruption that complements corticospinal tract measures ref [63]. Resting-state EEG also yields prognostic information: increased slow-wave activity and reduced alpha-band coherence over affected sensorimotor regions are associated with worse motor status, whereas normalization of spectral power and connectivity accompanies recovery ref [64], ref [65].

MEG has additionally revealed that recovery depends not only on focal reactivation of primary motor cortex but also on large-scale reconfiguration of distributed motor networks. Task-related beta modulation and cortico-cortical coherence in perilesional and bilateral sensorimotor regions have been related to hand function and longitudinal improvement ref [66], ref [67]. Because EEG is inexpensive and portable, and MEG offers superior source localization for oscillatory biomarkers, these modalities are increasingly used to stratify patients, monitor neurorehabilitation, and guide brain-computer interface or neuromodulation interventions ref [62], ref [68].

subsections.section_title: Noninvasive Brain Imaging Modalities for Assessing Motor Recovery
subsections.subsection_title: Functional near-infrared spectroscopy and portable imaging
subsections.content:
Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) provides a portable, motion-tolerant means of quantifying task-evoked and resting-state cortical hemodynamics, making it attractive for studying upper-limb recovery in stroke when conventional MRI is impractical. By measuring changes in oxy- and deoxyhemoglobin over superficial cortex, fNIRS can track recruitment of ipsilesional sensorimotor areas, compensatory contralesional activation, and therapy-related reorganization during ecologically valid movements such as reaching or grasping ref [69], ref [70].

Stroke studies using fNIRS have shown altered hemispheric balance and impaired interregional coupling during motor tasks, with patterns varying by lesion severity and chronicity. Early work demonstrated feasible monitoring of cortical sensorimotor activation during rehabilitative training after stroke ref [71], while later studies linked motor impairment to abnormal resting-state functional connectivity within motor networks measured by fNIRS ref [72]. Because recordings can be acquired during standing, walking, or robot-assisted therapy, portable optical imaging is particularly useful for probing recovery under naturalistic conditions that are difficult to reproduce in scanner-based paradigms ref [73].

Recent developments extend this approach beyond stationary cap-based systems. Wearable high-density diffuse optical tomography improves spatial sampling of perilesional cortex and supports repeated bedside measurements, potentially enabling longitudinal biomarkers of treatment response ref [74]. More broadly, mobile brain/body imaging frameworks that combine fNIRS with EEG and kinematics offer a route to multimodal monitoring of motor recovery in real-world rehabilitation settings ref [75]. Key limitations remain shallow penetration, susceptibility to extracerebral blood-flow artifacts, and lower anatomical specificity than fMRI, but fNIRS is emerging as an important complementary modality for prognostic stratification and therapy monitoring after stroke ref [70], ref [74].

subsections.section_title: Noninvasive Brain Imaging Modalities for Assessing Motor Recovery
subsections.subsection_title: Neuroimaging biomarkers for prognosis and stratification
subsections.content:
A central goal of post-stroke neuroimaging is to identify biomarkers that predict spontaneous recovery and stratify patients for specific interventions. Structural measures are among the most mature: damage to the corticospinal tract (CST), whether quantified by lesion overlap or diffusion-based integrity metrics, is strongly associated with upper-limb impairment and future recovery potential ref [76], ref [77]. This principle underlies clinically oriented frameworks such as the PREP algorithm, in which neurophysiological and imaging markers are combined to estimate likely motor outcome early after stroke ref [51].

Functional imaging adds complementary prognostic information by indexing the residual capacity of distributed motor networks. Early fMRI studies showed that recovery is related not simply to focal reactivation of ipsilesional primary motor cortex, but to dynamic reorganization across bilateral premotor, supplementary motor, and sensorimotor regions ref [78]. Resting-state connectivity measures further suggest that preservation or restoration of interhemispheric motor-network coupling tracks better behavioral outcome and may refine stratification beyond lesion anatomy alone ref [58].

Increasingly, multimodal models integrate structural injury, network physiology, and clinical deficits to define biologically grounded recovery subgroups. Large cohort work has emphasized that the proportional recovery rule is not universal and that patients with severe CST damage form a distinct low-recovery subgroup, supporting stratification by tract integrity rather than behavior alone ref [5]. The Stinear biomarker framework similarly argues for combining CST structure with corticomotor excitability and sensory-cognitive measures to guide prognosis and treatment selection ref [79], while broader reviews highlight multimodal prediction as a prerequisite for precision rehabilitation trials ref [80].

subsections.section_title: Noninvasive Brain Stimulation Techniques in Post-Stroke Motor Rehabilitation
subsections.subsection_title: Transcranial magnetic stimulation for motor recovery
subsections.content:
Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) is the most established focal brain-stimulation modality in post-stroke motor rehabilitation. By inducing brief magnetic fields over motor cortex, repetitive TMS (rTMS) can either increase cortical excitability when delivered at higher frequencies or intermittent theta-burst patterns, or suppress excitability when delivered at low frequencies. Early proof-of-concept studies showed that inhibitory 1 Hz stimulation of the contralesional primary motor cortex could improve paretic hand performance, consistent with attempts to reduce maladaptive interhemispheric inhibition after stroke ref [81], ref [82].

Subsequent trials expanded both targets and protocols. Facilitatory stimulation of ipsilesional motor cortex with high-frequency rTMS has been associated with gains in hand function and dexterity in selected patients with preserved corticospinal output ref [83]. Theta-burst stimulation offered a shorter protocol with similar mechanistic aims; intermittent theta-burst over ipsilesional motor areas improved motor practice effects in chronic stroke, whereas continuous theta-burst has been used contralesionally to downregulate excitability ref [84], ref [85]. Across studies, benefits are generally modest and heterogeneous, depending on lesion location, residual network integrity, baseline impairment, and coupling with task-specific therapy ref [86], ref [31].

Meta-analytic evidence supports a small-to-moderate positive effect of rTMS on upper-limb motor outcomes, particularly when stimulation is repeated over multiple sessions and integrated with rehabilitation practice ref [87]. Nevertheless, variability in response remains substantial, so contemporary use of TMS in stroke recovery increasingly emphasizes patient stratification, physiology-informed targeting, and protocol personalization rather than a single universal excitatory or inhibitory approach.

subsections.section_title: Noninvasive Brain Stimulation Techniques in Post-Stroke Motor Rehabilitation
subsections.subsection_title: Transcranial direct current stimulation and related electrical methods
subsections.content:
Transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) is the most widely studied electrical stimulation method in post-stroke motor rehabilitation. It delivers weak constant currents through scalp electrodes to bias cortical excitability: anodal stimulation over ipsilesional primary motor cortex is generally used to facilitate residual corticospinal output, whereas cathodal stimulation over contralesional motor cortex is intended to reduce excessive interhemispheric inhibition; bilateral montages combine both aims. Early mechanistic work in healthy participants established polarity-dependent shifts in motor cortical excitability and their dependence on stimulation duration, providing the physiological rationale for stroke applications [1,2].

Clinical studies suggest that tDCS can modestly improve upper-limb impairment or motor learning, particularly when paired with task-oriented practice, robotic therapy, or constraint-based training, although effects are heterogeneous across lesion location, chronicity, and baseline impairment [3,4]. Randomized studies have reported gains with both anodal ipsilesional and cathodal contralesional approaches, but larger multicenter trials and meta-analyses indicate small average effect sizes and substantial between-study variability, underscoring the need for individualized targeting rather than a single canonical montage [5,6].

Related transcranial electrical stimulation methods aim to refine or extend these effects. Transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) seeks to entrain oscillatory activity, while transcranial random noise stimulation (tRNS) may enhance excitability through stochastic resonance-like mechanisms; both remain less validated than tDCS in stroke populations. More focal current delivery with high-definition tDCS has also been proposed to improve target engagement and reproducibility [7,8]. Overall, electrical stimulation is attractive because it is portable, inexpensive, and easily combined with therapy, but its clinical translation depends on better dose selection, biomarker-guided patient stratification, and rigorous sham-controlled trials.

subsections.section_title: Noninvasive Brain Stimulation Techniques in Post-Stroke Motor Rehabilitation
subsections.subsection_title: Stimulation targets and hemispheric models
subsections.content:
Selection of stimulation targets in post-stroke motor rehabilitation has been shaped by hemispheric models of network imbalance. The classic interhemispheric competition account proposes that stroke reduces excitability in ipsilesional primary motor cortex (M1) while disinhibiting the contralesional hemisphere, which then exerts excessive transcallosal inhibition onto the damaged motor system; this framework motivated facilitatory stimulation of ipsilesional M1 and inhibitory stimulation of contralesional M1 ref [96], ref [97]. Early physiological and behavioral studies using transcranial magnetic stimulation provided support for altered interhemispheric interactions after stroke and linked their normalization to better motor outcome ref [98], ref [99].

However, lesion burden and residual structural reserve strongly condition whether this canonical strategy is appropriate. The bimodal balance-recovery model argues that patients with substantial corticospinal tract damage may rely more on contralesional motor areas, whereas those with preserved reserve benefit most from restoring ipsilesional dominance ref [100]. This view is consistent with evidence that the relationship between contralesional recruitment and impairment is not uniformly maladaptive, but varies with severity and stage of recovery ref [101]. Consequently, stimulation targets have expanded beyond M1 to include premotor cortex, supplementary motor area, and cerebellum when these nodes are thought to support compensatory control or sensorimotor recalibration ref [102], ref [103].

Current practice therefore favors target selection guided by impairment severity, lesion location, corticospinal integrity, and the phase of recovery rather than a fixed hemispheric rule. In this framework, hemispheric models are best viewed as heuristics for stratification and network-informed personalization, not as universally applicable prescriptions.

subsections.section_title: Noninvasive Brain Stimulation Techniques in Post-Stroke Motor Rehabilitation
subsections.subsection_title: Dose, timing, and protocol optimization
subsections.content:
Optimization of noninvasive brain stimulation after stroke depends on dose parameters (intensity, frequency, current density, train duration, and number of sessions), but also on when stimulation is delivered relative to the biological stage of recovery and to behavioral practice. Across TMS studies, single-session physiological effects do not reliably predict clinical benefit; meta-analytic evidence instead suggests that repeated-session protocols are more likely to yield measurable motor gains, although effect sizes remain heterogeneous and sensitive to protocol design and patient selection ref [104], ref [105]. For tDCS, dose is similarly multidimensional: current strength and electrode montage interact with lesion anatomy, baseline impairment, and concomitant therapy, making simple “more is better” assumptions unreliable ref [106].

Timing appears particularly important. Early after stroke, cortical excitability and network organization are highly labile, which may create a favorable but also variable window for intervention; in contrast, chronic stroke may require stronger coupling to task-specific training to overcome established maladaptive patterns ref [107]. Several trials indicate that pairing stimulation with or immediately before motor practice can enhance training-related plasticity, consistent with state-dependent and Hebbian accounts of neuromodulation ref [108], ref [109]. These observations have motivated priming, sequential, and closed-loop approaches that seek to align stimulation with ongoing cortical activity rather than delivering fixed schedules.

Protocol optimization is therefore moving toward individualized dosing. Computational current-flow modeling for tDCS and lesion-informed targeting for TMS can reduce interindividual variability, while adaptive designs may help identify responders and optimal session numbers ref [110], ref [111]. Future studies should integrate neurophysiological biomarkers with rehabilitation dose to determine not only whether stimulation is given, but to whom, when, and in what behavioral context.

subsections.section_title: Noninvasive Brain Stimulation Techniques in Post-Stroke Motor Rehabilitation
subsections.subsection_title: Safety, tolerability, and contraindications
subsections.content:
Noninvasive brain stimulation is generally well tolerated in stroke rehabilitation when delivered within established safety parameters, but adverse-event profiles differ across modalities. For repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), the principal serious risk is seizure, although this is rare when contemporary frequency-, intensity-, and train-duration limits are respected; more common effects are transient scalp discomfort, headache, neck pain, and occasional vasovagal symptoms ref [112], ref [113]. Transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) has a lower acute risk profile, with itching, tingling, mild burning, erythema, and fatigue reported most often, and serious complications are uncommon in standard protocols up to conventional current densities and session durations ref [114], ref [115].

Stroke-specific safety assessment is nevertheless essential because lesion characteristics, cortical excitability, medications, and comorbid epilepsy may alter risk. Consensus recommendations emphasize screening for prior seizures, skull defects or craniotomy, implanted metallic or electronic devices, unstable medical illness, and drugs that substantially lower seizure threshold before TMS; hearing protection and careful monitoring during treatment are also advised ref [112], ref [116]. For tDCS, contraindications are fewer but include compromised skin integrity at electrode sites and caution with implanted stimulators, high current densities, or poorly controlled epilepsy ref [114], ref [115].

Tolerability also depends on protocol design. Higher-frequency rTMS, patterned stimulation, and greater stimulation intensities can increase discomfort or theoretical seizure risk, whereas gradual ramping, optimized coil positioning, and analgesic-free skin preparation can improve adherence ref [113], ref [116]. Across post-stroke studies, serious adverse events attributable to stimulation remain uncommon, supporting clinical use within guideline-concordant frameworks, but standardized adverse-event reporting and individualized risk-benefit appraisal remain necessary, particularly in the subacute phase and in patients with mixed motor-cognitive deficits ref [117], ref [118].

subsections.section_title: Noninvasive Brain Stimulation Techniques in Post-Stroke Motor Rehabilitation
subsections.subsection_title: Mechanistic basis of stimulation-induced plasticity
subsections.content:
The working premise of noninvasive brain stimulation in post-stroke rehabilitation is that externally applied currents or magnetic fields can bias synaptic plasticity within residual motor networks. Early human physiology studies established that high-frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) tends to increase corticospinal excitability, whereas low-frequency rTMS reduces it, consistent with long-term potentiation- and long-term depression-like processes ref [119]. For transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), polarity-dependent shifts in motor cortical excitability were demonstrated in healthy cortex, with anodal stimulation generally facilitating and cathodal stimulation suppressing excitability, effects that can outlast stimulation and depend partly on NMDA-receptor-mediated mechanisms ref [120], ref [121].

After stroke, these plasticity-like effects are interpreted at the systems level as a means to rebalance activity within distributed sensorimotor networks. The influential interhemispheric competition model proposed that excessive transcallosal inhibition from the contralesional hemisphere can suppress ipsilesional motor output, providing a rationale for excitatory stimulation of the affected hemisphere or inhibitory stimulation of the unaffected hemisphere ref [122]. However, later work emphasized that mechanisms are heterogeneous and lesion-dependent: recovery may rely on restoration of perilesional excitability, recruitment of alternate descending pathways, or modulation of large-scale connectivity rather than simple normalization of a single excitability metric ref [123], ref [124].

Mechanistically, stimulation-induced gains are therefore best viewed as state-dependent metaplastic effects that interact with behavioral training. Pairing stimulation with voluntary movement practice or task-oriented therapy may strengthen Hebbian coincidence between cortical activation and sensory feedback, while stimulation timing, baseline impairment, corticospinal tract integrity, and genetic factors influence whether plasticity is adaptive or negligible ref [125], ref [126]. This framework explains both the promise of brain stimulation as an adjunct to motor rehabilitation and the substantial inter-individual variability observed in clinical trials.

subsections.section_title: Imaging-Guided and Multimodal Intervention Strategies
subsections.subsection_title: Imaging-informed target selection for stimulation
subsections.content:
Imaging-informed target selection seeks to move neuromodulation beyond atlas-based heuristics by identifying lesion-aware and network-relevant stimulation sites. Structural MRI and diffusion imaging can delineate residual corticospinal and transcallosal pathways, while functional MRI can reveal preserved task-evoked activity and disrupted resting-state organization. Early work in post-stroke recovery showed that integrity of the ipsilesional corticospinal tract and motor network connectivity predicts responsiveness to therapy, motivating stimulation of nodes that remain anatomically connected and physiologically recruitable rather than simply targeting canonical M1 coordinates ref [127], ref [128].

In practice, imaging has been used to individualize stimulation targets according to each patient’s residual network architecture. For noninvasive stimulation, lesion mapping and neuronavigation can adjust scalp-based targets to spared premotor, supplementary motor, or perilesional sensorimotor cortex when primary motor cortex is structurally compromised. Connectivity-guided targeting has become especially influential, as stimulation effects appear to depend on the distributed network coupled to the stimulated site rather than local anatomy alone; this principle is well illustrated by connectivity-based TMS targeting approaches in other neuropsychiatric domains and is increasingly being translated to rehabilitation ref [129], ref [130].

A key implication is that imaging should inform not only where to stimulate, but also which patients are likely to benefit from a given target. Biomarker frameworks combining lesion burden, corticospinal tract integrity, and functional network state can stratify candidates for ipsilesional facilitation versus contralesional inhibition and support more principled target selection than one-size-fits-all protocols ref [131], ref [36], ref [132]. Emerging lesion-network mapping approaches further suggest that symptoms and recovery potential may be anchored in distributed circuits, offering a route toward circuit-based stimulation prescriptions that are both mechanistically grounded and patient specific ref [133].

subsections.section_title: Imaging-Guided and Multimodal Intervention Strategies
subsections.subsection_title: Concurrent and sequential imaging-stimulation paradigms
subsections.content:
Concurrent imaging-stimulation paradigms seek to observe network-level responses during neuromodulation, whereas sequential paradigms use imaging acquired before or after stimulation to define targets, stratify patients, or quantify plasticity. Simultaneous EEG-fMRI has been especially informative for linking stimulation-evoked electrophysiological changes to distributed hemodynamic effects, showing that noninvasive stimulation modulates large-scale networks rather than only the cortex beneath the electrode or coil ref [134], ref [135]. In parallel, simultaneous TMS-fMRI has demonstrated the feasibility of mapping causal propagation from a stimulated cortical site to connected motor and associative regions, thereby providing a mechanistic basis for network-oriented intervention design ref [136].

Sequential workflows are currently more practical in rehabilitation because they avoid the technical constraints and artifact burden of fully concurrent acquisition. Resting-state and task-based MRI obtained before treatment can identify preserved corticocortical and corticospinal substrates associated with response, while post-intervention imaging can test whether behavioral gains are accompanied by normalization or reorganization of functional connectivity ref [137], ref [138]. In stroke, connectivity between ipsilesional motor cortex and distributed motor networks has repeatedly emerged as a marker for selecting stimulation targets and timing therapy relative to spontaneous recovery ref [139].

Methodologically, the choice between concurrent and sequential designs reflects a trade-off between mechanistic specificity and clinical deployability. Concurrent paradigms offer temporal proximity to stimulation effects but require rigorous control of stimulation artifacts, safety constraints, and state dependence; sequential paradigms are easier to scale and integrate with repeated rehabilitation sessions, but infer rather than directly observe online neural responses. Hybrid approaches—such as MRI-guided targeting followed by bedside EEG-monitored stimulation—may therefore provide the most translational compromise for personalized neurorehabilitation ref [135], ref [140], ref [141].

subsections.section_title: Imaging-Guided and Multimodal Intervention Strategies
subsections.subsection_title: Combination with task-oriented and robotic rehabilitation
subsections.content:
A central rationale for combining stimulation with task-oriented or robotic rehabilitation is that neuromodulation may transiently increase the excitability of spared motor networks, while intensive, goal-directed practice shapes those networks through use-dependent plasticity. This logic has been explored most extensively in stroke, where pairing noninvasive brain stimulation with occupational or upper-limb training has been used to strengthen task-specific gains rather than relying on stimulation as a standalone treatment ref [142], ref [143]. In this framework, imaging can further refine intervention timing and target selection by identifying residual corticospinal integrity, lesion-topography constraints, or compensatory recruitment patterns that determine whether patients are more likely to benefit from ipsilesional facilitation, contralesional suppression, or bilateral strategies.

Robotic devices provide a particularly attractive partner because they deliver high-dose, quantifiable, and repeatable practice while also generating kinematic and kinetic biomarkers that can be linked to neurophysiological state. Clinical studies have paired transcranial direct current stimulation with robot-assisted arm training after stroke, reporting feasibility and, in some cohorts, enhanced motor improvement relative to robotic therapy alone ref [144], ref [145]. Related work has combined gait robotics with spinal or cortical stimulation in people with spinal cord injury, showing that stimulation can increase the responsiveness of spinal locomotor circuits during intensive stepping practice and thereby support recovery-oriented training paradigms ref [146], ref [147].

However, the effects of these combinations are not uniformly synergistic. Large multicenter studies of intensive upper-limb training indicate substantial benefits from behavioral practice itself, setting a high bar for additive effects from stimulation ref [148]. Accordingly, future multimodal protocols will likely depend on better stratification and state-dependent dosing, integrating imaging, electrophysiology, and robotic performance metrics to determine not only who should receive combined therapy, but also when stimulation should be delivered relative to movement attempts, error augmentation, or assistance-as-needed control ref [149].

subsections.section_title: Imaging-Guided and Multimodal Intervention Strategies
subsections.subsection_title: Closed-loop and adaptive neuromodulation approaches
subsections.content:
Closed-loop and adaptive neuromodulation seeks to move beyond fixed stimulation schedules by updating stimulation timing, intensity, or location according to ongoing neural or behavioral state. In rehabilitation, this is attractive because corticospinal excitability, oscillatory phase, and network engagement vary substantially across and within sessions, limiting the reproducibility of open-loop protocols. Early demonstrations of EEG-triggered TMS showed that stimulation contingent on sensorimotor rhythms is technically feasible and can differentially modulate corticospinal output relative to non-contingent delivery ref [150], while phase-specific stimulation studies further indicated that the instantaneous state of the motor system shapes stimulation efficacy ref [151].

More recent work has operationalized this concept using explicit biomarkers for adaptive control. EEG-defined brain states have been used to gate transcranial current stimulation in real time ref [152], and phase-locked cortical stimulation has been shown to bidirectionally tune human beta oscillations ref [153]. At the invasive end, adaptive deep brain stimulation for Parkinson disease has provided a clinically important proof of principle that biomarker-driven stimulation can outperform conventional continuous paradigms while reducing unnecessary stimulation, particularly when beta-band activity is used as the control signal ref [154], ref [155].

For imaging-guided rehabilitation, the next step is integrating electrophysiology with functional imaging and kinematic feedback so that stimulation is adapted not only to oscillatory state but also to distributed network recruitment and task performance. Such multimodal closed-loop systems are increasingly plausible given real-time fMRI neurofeedback frameworks ref [156] and broader methodological roadmaps for feedback-controlled noninvasive stimulation ref [157]. Key challenges remain the stability of biomarkers, control latency, and demonstrating genuine synergistic gains over well-tuned open-loop therapy.

subsections.section_title: Imaging-Guided and Multimodal Intervention Strategies
subsections.subsection_title: Multimodal biomarkers for personalized therapy
subsections.content:
Multimodal biomarkers are increasingly used to stratify patients and tailor imaging-guided neuromodulation and rehabilitation. Rather than relying on lesion location or behavioral severity alone, personalized therapy can integrate structural injury, network integrity, and physiological reserve. In stroke, corticospinal tract damage measured with diffusion MRI and transcallosal or corticomotor physiology assessed with TMS provide complementary information about residual motor system capacity, helping distinguish patients likely to benefit from excitatory, inhibitory, or compensatory stimulation strategies ref [158], ref [159].

A prominent framework is the biomarker-based stratification proposed by the PREP and PREP2 algorithms, which combine simple clinical examination with TMS and, when needed, diffusion MRI to predict upper-limb recovery potential and thereby guide treatment intensity and goals ref [51], ref [160]. At a broader systems level, resting-state functional connectivity has emerged as a candidate marker of treatment responsiveness: preservation or restoration of interhemispheric motor network connectivity correlates with motor outcome after stroke and may identify patients most likely to respond to network-targeted stimulation ref [161], ref [162].

Recent work also suggests that biomarker integration should move beyond single modalities toward composite signatures. Large-scale analyses indicate that the effect of noninvasive brain stimulation depends on baseline impairment and structural reserve rather than one-size-fits-all protocols ref [163]. More generally, precision medicine frameworks in neurorehabilitation argue for combining imaging, electrophysiology, and behavioral phenotyping to define biologically coherent subgroups and adapt intervention parameters over time ref [164]. A key challenge is prospective validation of such multimodal models across sites, devices, and recovery stages before routine clinical deployment.

subsections.section_title: Imaging-Guided and Multimodal Intervention Strategies
subsections.subsection_title: Evaluation of synergistic versus additive treatment effects
subsections.content:
A central methodological issue in multimodal neurorehabilitation is whether combined interventions produce merely additive benefits or true synergy, i.e., gains exceeding the sum of each component delivered alone. Establishing this distinction requires factorial or multi-arm designs with interaction testing, because positive results from a combined protocol alone cannot distinguish mechanistic cooperation from simple accumulation of effects. This point is especially salient in stroke rehabilitation, where spontaneous recovery, task repetition, and inter-individual variability can inflate apparent combination benefits if proper comparator arms are absent ref [165], ref [166].

Evidence to date suggests that synergy is plausible but inconsistent, and often depends on timing, dose, and patient stratification. For example, pairing vagus nerve stimulation with rehabilitative training improved upper-limb outcomes in chronic stroke, supporting the idea that neuromodulation can enhance training-dependent plasticity rather than acting independently ref [167], ref [168]. By contrast, broader analyses of noninvasive brain stimulation combined with motor practice report heterogeneous effects, with substantial sensitivity to lesion characteristics, stimulation parameters, and behavioral context ref [93], ref [169]. These observations argue against treating combination therapy effects as uniform across populations.

Accordingly, evaluation frameworks should move beyond endpoint comparisons and quantify interaction at behavioral and biomarker levels. Imaging and electrophysiology can test whether combined interventions induce network reorganization, corticospinal recruitment, or state-dependent changes not observed with either modality alone. Recent consensus efforts also emphasize the need for prespecified mechanistic hypotheses, adequate sham/control conditions, and individualized target engagement measures when interpreting combined intervention trials ref [170], ref [171].

subsections.section_title: Clinical Evidence, Outcome Measures, and Translational Challenges
subsections.subsection_title: Evidence from clinical trials and systematic evaluations
subsections.content:
Clinical trials of noninvasive imaging- and stimulation-informed post-stroke motor rehabilitation show encouraging but uneven efficacy. For upper-limb recovery, large randomized studies of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) have reported modest gains when stimulation is added to conventional therapy, but effects vary with lesion location, chronicity, and stimulation target [1]. Similarly, transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) has shown small average benefits in some trials, yet multicenter evidence has not consistently demonstrated superiority over intensive therapy alone [2]. This pattern suggests that stimulation may act primarily as an adjunct whose value depends on appropriate patient selection and dosing.

Systematic evaluations reinforce this cautious interpretation. Meta-analyses of noninvasive brain stimulation after stroke generally identify statistically significant but clinically modest improvements in motor impairment, with substantial heterogeneity across protocols and populations [3,4]. Reviews of tDCS specifically note that positive findings are more common in small single-center studies than in larger, methodologically rigorous trials, raising concerns about publication bias and inflated early effect estimates [5]. In parallel, neuroimaging studies using fMRI and related methods have clarified mechanisms of reorganization and informed biomarker development, but imaging endpoints have not yet translated into robust treatment-selection tools for routine care [6].

Overall, the clinical evidence supports proof of concept rather than definitive effectiveness. Practice guidelines and consensus statements therefore recommend restrained interpretation, emphasizing standardized outcomes, sham-controlled designs, and stratification by impairment severity and corticospinal tract integrity before broad implementation is justified [7,8].

subsections.section_title: Clinical Evidence, Outcome Measures, and Translational Challenges
subsections.subsection_title: Outcome measures in motor rehabilitation research
subsections.content:
Outcome selection critically shapes conclusions about post-stroke motor rehabilitation, because different measures capture impairment, activity, participation, and real-world arm use at different levels of the International Classification of Functioning. The Fugl-Meyer Assessment remains the most widely used index of motor impairment and has strong psychometric support in stroke populations ref [180]. For upper-limb activity, the Action Research Arm Test and Wolf Motor Function Test are frequently used because they are responsive to change and complement impairment scales by indexing task performance and movement time ref [181], ref [182].

A central methodological issue is that gains on impairment scales do not always translate into meaningful increases in spontaneous limb use in daily life. This concern motivated use of the Motor Activity Log, which targets perceived amount and quality of affected-arm use outside the laboratory ref [183]. More recently, wearable sensors have been proposed to quantify real-world movement continuously and to address the limited ecological validity of clinic-based tests; accelerometry studies show that laboratory recovery and everyday arm use can diverge substantially after stroke ref [184].

Because treatment effects may be domain-specific, consensus recommendations emphasize multimodal outcome batteries, explicit timing of assessments, and prespecified clinically important differences rather than reliance on a single endpoint ref [185]. For walking-related recovery, measures such as gait speed and the 6-minute walk test capture distinct constructs and are linked to community ambulation and endurance ref [186], ref [187]. In trials of imaging-guided or stimulation-based interventions, combining standardized behavioral scales with kinematic and sensor-derived measures is therefore essential for detecting mechanistic effects while preserving clinical interpretability.

subsections.section_title: Clinical Evidence, Outcome Measures, and Translational Challenges
subsections.subsection_title: Patient heterogeneity and responder variability
subsections.content:
Post-stroke motor recovery is highly heterogeneous, and this variability strongly conditions the apparent efficacy of both noninvasive imaging biomarkers and stimulation-based interventions. Clinical response depends on lesion location and volume, time since stroke, baseline impairment, corticospinal tract integrity, and the balance of residual activity across hemispheres rather than on diagnosis alone. The proportional recovery literature highlighted that initial impairment constrains achievable gains, although subsequent debate has also underscored the risk of oversimplified recovery rules and the need for richer stratification models ref [1], ref [2].

For stimulation studies, responder variability is particularly evident when neurophysiological reserve is limited. The PREP algorithm and related work showed that simple clinical measures combined with transcranial magnetic stimulation and diffusion imaging can stratify upper-limb outcome according to corticospinal tract integrity ref [3]. In parallel, the bimodal balance-recovery model proposed that some patients may benefit from rebalancing interhemispheric inhibition, whereas those with extensive structural damage may rely on compensatory recruitment of ipsilesional and contralesional resources ref [4]. These frameworks help explain why trials of ostensibly similar transcranial direct current stimulation or repetitive TMS protocols often yield inconsistent average effects.

Imaging-based markers may improve patient selection, but they also reveal that stroke is not a single-network disorder. Damage to distributed structural and functional networks, including disconnection of critical hubs, contributes to interindividual differences in impairment and treatment responsiveness ref [5], ref [6]. This has motivated precision rehabilitation approaches that subtype patients using behavioral and neuroimaging features rather than broad clinical categories ref [7], while recent consensus recommendations emphasize adequate sample sizes, prespecified effect modifiers, and stratified analyses to distinguish true nonresponse from poor matching of therapy to biology ref [8].

subsections.section_title: Clinical Evidence, Outcome Measures, and Translational Challenges
subsections.subsection_title: Methodological limitations and reproducibility concerns
subsections.content:
A persistent limitation in post-stroke imaging and stimulation studies is inadequate statistical power. Small, single-center trials dominate the literature, increasing effect-size inflation, false positives, and instability of subgroup findings. These concerns are amplified when heterogeneous lesion profiles, chronicity, and concomitant therapies are analyzed in underpowered samples, a broader problem highlighted across neuroscience and brain stimulation research ref [188], ref [189]. In noninvasive stimulation, inconsistent sham conditions, incomplete blinding, and variable reporting of allocation concealment further complicate causal inference and comparison across trials ref [190], ref [191].

Reproducibility is also weakened by substantial protocol heterogeneity. Imaging endpoints vary from task-based activation and resting-state connectivity to diffusion metrics and lesion-network approaches, while stimulation studies differ in montage, intensity, timing relative to therapy, and dose accumulation. Even apparently minor differences in electrode placement or current modeling can alter target engagement, undermining cross-study comparability ref [192]. More generally, analytical flexibility, selective outcome reporting, and weak standardization in MRI acquisition and preprocessing remain recognized threats to reliable biomarker discovery and validation ref [193], ref [194].

Improving translation will require prospective registration, adequately powered multicenter designs, harmonized core outcome sets, transparent adverse-event reporting, and routine sharing of protocols, code, and de-identified imaging derivatives. Consensus-oriented methodological guidance in both neuroimaging and stimulation provides a practical foundation, but adherence remains uneven ref [191], ref [194], ref [195].

subsections.section_title: Clinical Evidence, Outcome Measures, and Translational Challenges
subsections.subsection_title: Implementation in clinical workflows
subsections.content:
Implementation of noninvasive imaging and stimulation in routine post-stroke rehabilitation depends less on proof-of-concept efficacy than on whether protocols can be embedded into existing therapy pathways, staffing models, and time constraints. Clinical uptake is favored by brief acquisition or stimulation sessions, standardized operating procedures, and compatibility with multidisciplinary stroke services rather than stand-alone research workflows. In practice, this means that candidate tools must show incremental value over conventional assessment and therapy, not only statistical effects in controlled trials ref [196], ref [197].

Workflow integration also requires attention to training, safety screening, and treatment fidelity. Consensus guidance for transcranial magnetic and electrical stimulation has emphasized operator competency, contraindication screening, dose specification, and adverse-event monitoring as prerequisites for scalable use ref [112], ref [198]. For imaging-based stratification, translational feasibility is strongest when biomarkers can be derived from routinely available modalities such as structural MRI or standard TMS measures of corticospinal tract integrity, rather than highly specialized protocols that are difficult to schedule repeatedly in rehabilitation settings ref [199], ref [200].

A further challenge is aligning intervention timing and outcome tracking with real-world recovery trajectories. Stroke rehabilitation pathways are heterogeneous across acute, inpatient, and outpatient settings, and biomarker-informed approaches such as the proportional recovery and PREP-style frameworks illustrate both the promise and logistical demands of tailoring therapy intensity and stimulation targets to individual impairment profiles ref [201], ref [51]. Consequently, successful implementation will likely require pragmatic trials, interoperable data capture, and reimbursement models that recognize imaging- and stimulation-guided personalization as part of routine rehabilitative care rather than an adjunct research activity.

subsections.section_title: Clinical Evidence, Outcome Measures, and Translational Challenges
subsections.subsection_title: Ethical, regulatory, and future translational directions
subsections.content:
Ethical translation of noninvasive imaging- and stimulation-guided post-stroke rehabilitation requires balancing innovation with uncertain individual benefit. Safety frameworks for transcranial magnetic stimulation and transcranial direct current stimulation emphasize screening for seizure risk, implanted devices, medication interactions, and careful adverse-event monitoring, which is especially important in older, medically complex stroke populations ref [112], ref [202]. Beyond procedural safety, equitable access is a central concern: technologies that depend on advanced neuroimaging, neuronavigation, or repeated supervised sessions may preferentially benefit patients treated at well-resourced centers, widening disparities unless simplified and scalable pathways are developed.

Regulatory progress also depends on evidence standards that are often stronger than those used in early mechanistic studies. International recommendations for stroke recovery trials have argued for clearer intervention dosing, biologically informed stratification, prespecified outcomes, and multicenter designs to support clinical adoption ref [203]. More broadly, development of biomarkers for treatment selection must satisfy requirements for analytical validity, clinical validity, and clinical utility before they can justify regulatory or reimbursement decisions ref [204]. The mixed efficacy literature for stimulation after stroke further underscores the need for sham rigor, reproducible protocols, and transparent reporting before routine implementation ref [205], ref [206].

Future translational directions will likely combine precision rehabilitation with pragmatic delivery. Imaging and neurophysiology may help identify responder subgroups, but predictive models should be prospectively validated and tested for transportability across sites and impairment strata ref [204], ref [207]. At the same time, large simple trials, embedded rehabilitation studies, and consensus-based reporting standards can improve generalizability and accelerate translation from laboratory efficacy to service-level effectiveness ref [203], ref [208].
